SUMMARY:Crossroads of America: Oklahoma's Route 66 screening
DESCRIPTION:On Tuesday\, October 27\, at 6 p.m.\, there will be a free screening of the new documentary Crossroads of America: Oklahoma’s Route 66 at the Centre Theatre in El Reno. \nThe Oklahoma Historical Society\, in collaboration with director Bryan Beasley\, producers Jon and Jaime Roman\, and with support from the Inasmuch Foundation\, has produced Crossroads of America: Oklahoma’s Route 66. This documentary examines the evolution of Route 66 in Oklahoma\, from the hardships of the Dust Bowl era to post-WWII road trips. It explores the highway’s history and future through interviews with historians\, interactions with small-business owners\, and scenes created using virtual production technology filmed at the Cherokee Film Studios. \nVisit crossroadsok66.com/ to learn more. \n

SUMMARY:Sorting out Race: Examining Racial Identity and Stereotypes in Thrift Store Donations exhibit closes
DESCRIPTION:The Cherokee Strip Regional Heritage Center’s traveling exhibition\, Sorting out Race: Examining Racial Identity and Stereotypes in Thrift Store Donations\, will close on Friday\, October 30.\n\nThis exhibition explores controversial themes and displays racially offensive images to stimulate a healthy community conversation about our ongoing struggles with race. \nEvery day\, thrift stores receive items with racial imagery—antique advertising cards\, collectible salt-and-pepper shakers\, vintage children’s books\, and mugs with sports team mascots. This exhibit asks questions: \n\n“Are these harmless reminders of past attitudes\, or do they perpetuate stereotypes about race?”\n“Should thrift stores sell these objects? Or should they be ‘sorted out’ of the resale environment and discarded?”\n\nSorting Out Race arose out of a desire to divert artifacts with racial content from thrift stores to an exhibit that would generate a healthy community conversation about racial stereotypes\, past and present\, in order to heighten awareness of our continuing struggles with race. \nKauffman Museum formed the Thrift Store Collection from items found at thrift shops in Kansas between 2010 and 2015. \nThis traveling exhibition was designed and produced by Kauffman Museum at Bethel College in North Newton\, Kansas. The exhibit team: Nicole Eitzen\, Jacob Harris\, David Kreider\, Annette LeZotte\, Paloma Olais\, Rachel Pannabecker\, Chuck Regier. Original exhibit concept by Leia Lawrence. \nThe Sorting Out Race exhibit is included in the museum admission at no additional cost. \n \n
URL:https://www.okhistory.org/calendar/event/sorting-out-race-examining-racial-identity-and-stereotypes-in-thrift-store-donations-exhibit-closes/

SUMMARY:Addie's Trunk exhibit closes
DESCRIPTION:The Fred and Addie Drummond Home invites you to step back in time in October with a new exhibit that brings to life the ways women in the early 1900s carefully packed for long journeys. \nThe exhibit showcases Addie Drummond’s coats\, dresses\, hats\, and accessories\, thoughtfully arranged as if awaiting a grand adventure. Women of this era would have traveled with massive trunks\, some tipping the scales at over 100 pounds\, brimming with quilts\, sunbonnets\, and cherished Sunday outfits\, each chosen for both elegance and necessity. Setting out for a visit to a homestead required readiness for shifting weather and meant packing layers of clothing\, from sturdy corsets to flowing petticoats. \nThroughout October\, visitors to the Fred and Addie Drummond Home can observe these historic travel treasures and imagine the stark differences between journeys of the past and the conveniences of travel today. \n \n
URL:https://www.okhistory.org/calendar/event/addies-trunk-exhibit-closes/

SUMMARY:Lonesome Dove Photo Exhibit closes
DESCRIPTION:The Museum of the Western Prairie will host the Lonesome Dove Photo Exhibit through Saturday\, October 31. \nLonesome Dove—Larry McMurtry’s epic novel of two aging Texas Rangers who drive a herd of stolen cattle 2\,500 miles from the Rio Grande to Montana to found the first ranch there—captured the public imagination and has never let it go. The Lonesome Dove miniseries\, which first aired on CBS in 1989\, lassoed an even wider audience. \nCapturing the sweeping visual imagery of the original miniseries\, the Lonesome Dove exhibition presents fifty-five framed classic images taken during filming by Bill Wittliff\, a renowned photographer\, writer\, and executive producer (with Suzanne De Passe) of Lonesome Dove. The images\, however\, are worlds apart from ordinary production stills\, depicting an extraordinary union of art\, literature\, and history. \nThe exhibit travels to Altus in partnership with Humanities Texas\, the state affiliate for the National Endowment for the Humanities. \nGus and Call on the Mesa\, © 1988\, Bill Wittliff. The Lonesome Dove miniseries stars Robert Duvall as Augustus McCrae and Tommy Lee Jones as Woodrow Call. The Oscar-winning actors portray aging Texas Rangers who lead an epic cattle drive from Texas to Montana in the late 1800s. \n
URL:https://www.okhistory.org/calendar/event/lonesome-dove-photo-exhibit-closes/

SUMMARY:“Washington Irving and the Mounted Rangers” program
DESCRIPTION:On Saturdays\, October 17\, 24\, and 31\, from 10 a.m. to noon\, and again from 1 to 4 p.m.\, the Fort Gibson Historic Site staff will hold a come-and-go living history program to educate the public about early expeditions to Fort Gibson in 1832. \nThat year\, author Washington Irving arrived at Fort Gibson\, which was the last stop on his journey to explore the western frontier. He also traveled with a unique group of Mounted Rangers. During his time with Captain Bean’s company of Mounted Rangers\, Irving gathered the materials for his book A Tour on the Prairies (1835)\, one of the first written accounts of daily life on the western prairie and one that reached many American readers in the East. \nSite interpreter Seth Goff will demonstrate the Mounted Rangers’ equipment\, some of Irving’s equipment he brought as an author\, and survival skills practiced by all expedition members. \nThe program is included with admission. Interested guests should check in at the Palisade admissions office located across the parade square from the entrance gate. This program is conducted outside of climate-controlled areas\, so please dress accordingly for October weather. \n \n
URL:https://www.okhistory.org/calendar/event/washington-irving-and-the-mounted-rangers/2026-10-31/

SUMMARY:We Fought Back: The Black Legal Struggle for Education in Oklahoma Territory book talk and signing with author Sara Doolittle
DESCRIPTION:Author Dr. Sara Doolittle will present a free author talk and book signing at The Chisholm on Thursday\, November 5\, at 6 p.m. The discussion will feature her new title\, We Fought Back: The Black Legal Struggle for Education in Oklahoma Territory (The University of Oklahoma Press\, 2026). Copies of the book will be available at the signing. \nMost people are familiar with the landmark 1954 US Supreme Court decision Brown v. Board of Education\, which held that state laws mandating racial segregation in public schools were unconstitutional. But what about the court cases that far preceded\, and informed\, this national ruling? They took place in smaller courts\, in unsung parts of the United States\, including in Oklahoma Territory. There\, decades before Brown v. Board of Education\, Black citizens worked to challenge legislation and local school board restrictions that segregated their schools. In We Fought Back\, Sara Doolittle analyzes a rich array of previously unexplored court challenges during Oklahoma’s territorial period (1889–1907)\, revealing how Black residents’ cases reshaped understandings of race\, citizenship\, and the federal role in American schooling. \nAbout the author\nSara Doolittle is an assistant professor in the Department of Educational Sciences\, Foundations\, and Research at the University of Central Oklahoma. Her scholarship explores the intersection of law\, race\, and schooling\, with a particular focus on 19th-century school segregation law. Her research on legal challenges to Oklahoma’s territorial segregation statutes has appeared in History of Education Quarterly\, and her forthcoming book is We Fought Back: The Black Legal Struggle for Education in Oklahoma Territory. She is a recipient of both the National Academy of Education/Spencer Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship and Dissertation Research Award. Doolittle brings more than two decades of experience as a high school English teacher to her work. A proud product of public schools\, she earned her BA from the University of Kansas\, her MA from the University of Colorado\, and her PhD from the University of Oklahoma. \n

SUMMARY:“Cards and Board Games: Entertainment in the 1830s” program
DESCRIPTION:A living history program held on Saturday\, November 7\, 14\, and 21 will explore entertainment in the 1830s. Site interpreter Seth Goff will demonstrate and teach visitors how games were set up and played. You can learn more about how 19th-century soldiers and civilians entertained themselves with faro and card games. \nWhenever the soldiers at Fort Gibson had authorized downtime—or whenever enlisted soldiers decided to take a “break” at the expense of Uncle Sam and their officers\, there were many options for entertainment during downtime. Gambling card games like faro\, as well as more innocent games like checkers\, dominoes\, and others\, were commonly played by both soldiers and civilians in the 1830s. \nPlease check in at the Palisade admissions office located across the parade square from the entrance gate. This program is conducted outside of climate-controlled areas\, so visitors should dress for unpredictable weather in November. \n \n

SUMMARY:History Alive! on the Cherokee Strip
DESCRIPTION:Step back in time and experience life in the Cherokee Outlet during History Alive! on the Cherokee Strip\, a living history program at the Cherokee Strip Regional Heritage Center in Enid. \nIt takes place throughout the year on the first and third Saturday of each month from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. The five historic buildings in the Humphrey Heritage Village\, dating back to the territorial era\, come to life with living history interpreters dressed in period clothing from the late 1800s. Attendees can sit at school desks in the 1896 Turkey Creek one-room schoolhouse while lessons are taught\, hear a pioneer tale from those tending their shops\, and watch as craftsmen and women work their trades. Visitors can step inside the 1905 Glidewell house or stop by the 1902 church. Guests can watch and participate in the different skills and trades of the time or file their own land claim at the historic 1893 US Land Office. A one-room log cabin\, built in 1900 by the Sneed family after the Cherokee Outlet Opening in 1893\, has been rebuilt on site. \nHistory Alive! began as a monthly program in the winter of 2019\, and has grown into a bimonthly event. Volunteers are always needed. \nPlan your visit! \n

SUMMARY:Vietnam War: Untold Stories from the South—Trials\, Triumphs\, & Tragedies documentary screening
DESCRIPTION:A powerful new documentary that centers on the lived experiences and overlooked perspectives of South Vietnam and the Vietnamese diaspora will be shown at the Oklahoma History Center on Saturday\, November 7\, from 1 to 3 p.m. \nThe Vietnam War: Untold Stories from the South — Trials\, Triumphs\, & Tragedies (2025) documentary reexamines the war through the experiences of South Vietnamese civilians\, soldiers\, political prisoners\, refugees\, and families whose stories have too often been overlooked\, distorted\, or excluded from mainstream historical narratives. Drawing on extensive research\, archival materials\, and firsthand testimony\, the film explores communist land reform\, wartime violence\, political persecution\, media bias\, reeducation camps\, the refugee exodus\, and the conflict’s lasting human consequences. Central to the documentary is the historical argument that Hồ Chí Minh and the Vietnamese Communist Party began their campaign to conquer South Vietnam by force years before American combat troops arrived.  \nThe screening is free and open to the public\, but museum admission is required to visit the galleries. \nAbout the Producer: \nNam Pham\, the producer of Vietnam War: Untold Stories from the South — Trials\, Triumphs & Tragedies\, is a Vietnamese American documentary filmmaker\, author\, and community leader committed to preserving the history\, voices\, and lived experiences of the Vietnamese people. As Founder and President of the Next Vietnam Projects Foundation\, he leads documentary and educational initiatives that illuminate Vietnam’s modern history and affirm the enduring values of freedom\, human dignity\, and democracy. \n \n

SUMMARY:Kilgen Theatre Organ performance featuring the silent film My Best Girl (1927) with Clark Wilson
DESCRIPTION:On Monday\, November 9\, from 7 to 8:30 p.m.\, a Kilgen Theatre Organ performance will be held in the Devon Great Hall at the Oklahoma History Center\, featuring organist Clark Wilson accompanying the silent film My Best Girl (1927). \nMy Best Girl is a 1927 American silent romantic comedy film directed by Sam Taylor\, starring Mary Pickford and Charles “Buddy” Rogers. Charles Rosher received an Academy Award nomination for his cinematography of this film in 1928. \nClark Wilson is one of the most prominent and recognized scorers of silent photoplays in America today. He works exclusively with the organ to develop historically accurate musical accompaniments as they were performed in major picture palaces during the heyday of silent film. \nTickets are $10 for Oklahoma Historical Society members and $20 for the general public. They can be purchased by calling 405-522-0765. \nPurchase tickets online. \n \n

SUMMARY:Crossroads of America: Oklahoma’s Route 66 evening screening on OETA
DESCRIPTION:Crossroads of America: Oklahoma’s Route 66 will re-air on OETA on Thursday\, November 12\, at 7 p.m. \nThe Oklahoma Historical Society\, in collaboration with Director Bryan Beasley\, producers Jon and Jaime Roman\, and with support from the Inasmuch Foundation\, has produced Crossroads of America: Oklahoma’s Route 66. This documentary examines the evolution of Route 66 in Oklahoma\, from the hardships of the Dust Bowl era to post-WWII road trips. \nCrossroads of America: Oklahoma’s Route 66 reveals why Oklahoma is the heart of the Mother Road\, weaving together the rich history of America’s most iconic highway with the inspiring stories of the people who continue to live\, dream\, and shape Route 66’s next 100 years. \nAs Route 66 approaches its 100th anniversary\, Crossroads of America: Oklahoma’s Route 66 tells the remarkable story of how Oklahoma helped shape America’s most iconic highway\, and how the Mother Road\, in turn\, helped shape America itself. \nFrom Cy Avery’s vision that placed Oklahoma at the heart of Route 66 to the families who traveled west in search of opportunity\, the highway has always been more than a road. It became a pathway to the American Dream\, carrying Dust Bowl migrants toward new beginnings\, fueling generations of small-town entrepreneurs\, and welcoming post-war travelers in search of adventure\, freedom\, and possibility. \nThe film also celebrates Oklahoma legends whose stories became inseparable from Route 66. Will Rogers embodied the humor\, optimism\, and spirit of the open road\, while Woody Guthrie gave voice to those chasing a better life along it. Their legacies\, like the highway itself\, helped define the American experience. \nBlending rich history with deeply personal stories\, Crossroads of America follows the people who continue to live\, work\, and dream along Route 66 today. From restaurateurs and artists to preservationists and community leaders\, they are not only protecting the Mother Road’s remarkable legacy—they are shaping its next 100 years. \nAt its heart\, this is a story about the people. Their resilience\, determination\, and enduring belief in the promise of tomorrow remind us that Route 66 has never simply connected places; it has connected generations\, communities\, and dreams. \nDirector Bryan Beasley maintains a longstanding collaboration with the Oklahoma Historical Society. His career began with the acclaimed documentary Unconquered: Allan Houser and the Legacy of One Apache Family\, narrated by Val Kilmer\, and the historical narrative The Battle of Honey Springs. Beasley and Thompson further collaborated on the 2023 documentary The People’s House: The Story of the Oklahoma State Capitol. \n \n

SUMMARY:Inked in History
DESCRIPTION:Visit the Cherokee Strip Regional Heritage Center in Enid for its Inked in History event on Friday\, November 13\, from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the signing of Senate Bill 806. \nThe bill was signed by Governor Brad Henry and took effect on November 1\, 2006. It legalized tattooing in Oklahoma\, making it the last state to do so. At this special event\, visitors will learn about the history of tattooing in Oklahoma and its roots in Indigenous cultures. \nLocal tattoo artists from Culture Tattoo in Enid\, Spaded & Jaded in Tulsa\, and Nathalie Standingcloud from Tahlequah will be on hand to provide flash tattoos to those interested. Entry to this event is included in the regular museum admission fee. Those seeking a tattoo must be 18 years of age and present a valid ID. Tattoos are available on a first-come\, first-served basis and are subject to a separate fee payable to the artist. Some artists only accept cash. The Cherokee Strip Regional Heritage Center does not have an ATM on site\, so please be prepared in advance. \nCoffee Inclination will have their coffee trailer with drinks available for purchase during the Inked in History event. \nFor more information about the Cherokee Strip Regional Heritage Center\, please visit csrhc.org or call 580-237-1907. \n \n

SUMMARY:2026 Oklahoma Folklife Festival
DESCRIPTION:The Folklife Festival at the Oklahoma History Center will be held on Saturday\, November 14\, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. This event is free and open to the public. \nThis festival aims to engage visitors by providing opportunities to experience diverse cultures and traditions. Visitors will be encouraged to participate in various activities rather than just observe. The festival’s objectives include sparking curiosity\, facilitating intercultural exchange\, creating participatory experiences\, and collaborating with cultural practitioners\, communities\, and heritage professionals. The event will primarily take place indoors\, and admission will be free for the public. \n\n\n
